title: Cost Accounting I
source_note: Grounded in standard introductory cost accounting curriculum (cost classification, material/labour/overhead costing, job/batch/process costing, marginal costing, cost-volume-profit and break-even analysis) as taught in NUC-aligned Nigerian university accounting programmes.

questions.question: Costs that can be directly and wholly identified with, and traced to, a specific cost unit (e.g. the timber used in making a particular table) are called:
questions.explanation: Direct costs are costs that can be economically and specifically traced to a single cost unit, such as the direct material used in a product.

questions.question: Costs that cannot be traced to a specific cost unit but are incurred for the benefit of several cost units or the business as a whole are known as:
questions.explanation: Indirect costs, or overheads, cannot be conveniently and economically traced to a single cost unit and must instead be apportioned or absorbed across cost units.

questions.question: A cost that remains constant in total within a relevant range of activity, regardless of the level of output, is called a:
questions.explanation: Fixed costs, such as factory rent, do not change in total as output changes within the relevant range, although the fixed cost per unit falls as output rises.

questions.question: A cost that changes in direct proportion to the level of activity or output is called a:
questions.explanation: Variable costs, such as direct material, increase or decrease in total in direct proportion to output, while remaining constant per unit.

questions.question: Electricity bills that include a fixed standing charge plus a charge per unit of power consumed are an example of a:
questions.explanation: A semi-variable (mixed) cost has both a fixed element that does not change with activity and a variable element that changes with the level of activity, as with many utility bills.

questions.question: A company uses 1,000 units of a raw material per year. The cost of placing one order is ₦40 and the annual holding cost is ₦2 per unit. Using the Economic Order Quantity (EOQ) formula, the EOQ is:
questions.explanation: EOQ = square root of (2 x Annual demand x Ordering cost / Holding cost per unit) = sqrt(2 x 1,000 x 40 / 2) = sqrt(40,000) = 200 units.

questions.question: The reorder level of a stock item is calculated as:
options: Maximum usage rate multiplied by maximum lead time
Minimum usage rate multiplied by minimum lead time
Average usage rate divided by economic order quantity
Annual demand divided by number of orders per year
questions.correct_answer: Maximum usage rate multiplied by maximum lead time
questions.explanation: The reorder level is set high enough to cover the worst case of maximum usage during the maximum lead time, ensuring stock does not run out before the next delivery arrives.

questions.question: A store received 200 kg of material at ₦5 per kg, followed by 300 kg at ₦6 per kg. If 250 kg is issued to production and valued using the FIFO (first-in, first-out) method, the value of the issue is:
questions.explanation: Under FIFO, the 250 kg issued comprises the first 200 kg at ₦5 (₦1,000) plus 50 kg at ₦6 (₦300), giving a total issue value of ₦1,300.

questions.question: Using the same data (200 kg at ₦5, then 300 kg at ₦6, 250 kg issued), if the LIFO (last-in, first-out) method is used instead, the value of the closing stock is:
questions.explanation: Under LIFO, the 250 kg issued is taken entirely from the most recent 300 kg batch at ₦6 (₦1,500 issued), leaving closing stock of 200 kg at ₦5 plus 50 kg at ₦6 = 1,000 + 300 = ₦1,300.

questions.question: A worker is paid ₦20 per unit produced under a piece-rate system. If the worker produces 150 units in a day, total pay for the day is:
questions.explanation: Piece-rate pay = Units produced x Rate per unit = 150 x ₦20 = ₦3,000.

questions.question: Under the Halsey bonus scheme, the time allowed for a job is 10 hours, the time taken is 8 hours, and the hourly rate is ₦100. If the bonus is 50% of the time saved, the total pay for the job is:
questions.explanation: Time saved = 10 - 8 = 2 hours. Bonus = 50% x 2 x ₦100 = ₦100. Total pay = (Time taken x Rate) + Bonus = (8 x 100) + 100 = ₦900.

questions.question: Idle time in labour costing refers to:
options: Time paid for during which the worker performs no productive work, e.g. due to machine breakdown
Time spent by a worker on incentive-based tasks
Time taken to train a new employee
questions.correct_answer: Time paid for during which the worker performs no productive work, e.g. due to machine breakdown
questions.explanation: Idle time arises when employees are paid for time during which no output is produced, for reasons such as machine breakdowns, power failure, or waiting for materials.

questions.question: The extra amount paid to a worker for hours worked beyond the normal working hours, usually at a higher rate, is called:
questions.explanation: Overtime premium is the additional amount, above the normal hourly rate, paid for hours worked outside the normal working schedule.

questions.question: The process of charging whole items of overhead cost directly to a specific cost centre or cost unit, where the cost is clearly identifiable, is called overhead:
questions.explanation: Allocation is the charging of overhead costs that can be directly identified with a single cost centre in full, unlike apportionment, which shares common costs across several cost centres on some fair basis.

questions.question: The process of sharing a common overhead cost, such as factory rent, among several cost centres on a fair and reasonable basis (e.g. floor area occupied) is called overhead:
questions.explanation: Apportionment shares overhead costs that benefit more than one cost centre using an equitable basis, such as floor area for rent or number of employees for canteen costs.

questions.question: The process of charging overheads absorbed by a cost centre to the cost units (products or jobs) that pass through it, usually using a predetermined overhead absorption rate, is called overhead:
questions.explanation: Absorption is the final stage of overhead costing, where overheads accumulated in a cost centre are charged to (absorbed by) the products or jobs produced, using a rate such as per machine hour or per labour hour.

questions.question: A factory budgets total production overhead of ₦100,000 and budgeted machine hours of 5,000 for the period. The overhead absorption rate (OAR) per machine hour is:
questions.explanation: OAR = Budgeted overhead / Budgeted machine hours = ₦100,000 / 5,000 hours = ₦20 per machine hour.

questions.question: A job requires direct materials of ₦5,000, direct labour of ₦3,000, and uses 200 machine hours. If the overhead absorption rate is ₦20 per machine hour, the total cost of the job is:
questions.explanation: Overhead absorbed = 200 hours x ₦20 = ₦4,000. Total job cost = Direct material + Direct labour + Overhead absorbed = 5,000 + 3,000 + 4,000 = ₦12,000.

questions.question: Job costing is most appropriate for a business that:
options: Produces goods or services to specific customer orders, each with distinguishable characteristics
Produces a single homogeneous product continuously in large volumes
Only sells finished goods purchased from suppliers
Has no overhead costs to allocate
questions.correct_answer: Produces goods or services to specific customer orders, each with distinguishable characteristics
questions.explanation: Job costing accumulates costs separately for each distinct job or contract, making it suitable for businesses such as printers, builders, or repair workshops that carry out customer-specific work.

questions.question: Batch costing is best described as:
options: A form of job costing applied to a group (batch) of identical items produced together, with cost per unit found by dividing the total batch cost by the number of units
A method used only for continuous process industries like oil refining
A method that ignores overheads completely
The same as unit costing for a single item
questions.correct_answer: A form of job costing applied to a group (batch) of identical items produced together, with cost per unit found by dividing the total batch cost by the number of units
questions.explanation: Batch costing treats a batch of identical units as the cost unit, accumulating total cost for the batch and dividing by the number of units to find cost per unit, common in industries like shoe or garment manufacturing.

questions.question: In process costing, 1,000 kg of material is input to a process. Normal loss is expected to be 10% of input, and actual output is 850 kg (with no units in work-in-progress). The abnormal loss in kg is:
questions.explanation: Normal loss = 10% x 1,000 = 100 kg, so expected output = 1,000 - 100 = 900 kg. Since actual output is 850 kg, abnormal loss = 900 - 850 = 50 kg.

questions.question: In process costing, if actual output exceeds the expected output (input less normal loss), the difference is called:
questions.explanation: Abnormal gain arises when actual loss is less than the normal (expected) loss, so actual output is higher than the expected output figure.

questions.question: Prime cost in cost accounting is calculated as:
options: Direct materials + Direct labour + Direct expenses
Total cost - Selling and distribution overhead
questions.correct_answer: Direct materials + Direct labour + Direct expenses
questions.explanation: Prime cost is the aggregate of all direct costs of production: direct materials, direct labour, and any direct expenses specifically traceable to the cost unit.

questions.question: A product has direct material cost of ₦10,000, direct labour cost of ₦6,000, and direct expenses of ₦1,000. If factory overhead of ₦5,000 is added, the factory (works) cost is:
questions.explanation: Prime cost = 10,000 + 6,000 + 1,000 = ₦17,000. Factory (works) cost = Prime cost + Factory overhead = 17,000 + 5,000 = ₦22,000.

questions.question: In marginal costing, contribution is defined as:
options: Sales revenue minus total costs (including fixed costs)
questions.explanation: Contribution is the amount remaining from sales revenue after deducting variable costs, and it is available first to cover fixed costs and then to provide profit.

questions.question: A product sells for ₦50 per unit and has a variable cost of ₦30 per unit. Fixed costs for the period are ₦100,000. The break-even point in units is:
questions.explanation: Contribution per unit = 50 - 30 = ₦20. Break-even point (units) = Fixed costs / Contribution per unit = 100,000 / 20 = 5,000 units.

questions.question: Using the same data (selling price ₦50, variable cost ₦30, fixed cost ₦100,000), the break-even point in sales value (Naira) is:
questions.explanation: Break-even sales value = Break-even units x Selling price = 5,000 x ₦50 = ₦250,000.

questions.question: If a company's actual sales are 8,000 units and its break-even point is 5,000 units, the margin of safety is:
questions.explanation: Margin of safety = Actual (or budgeted) sales - Break-even sales = 8,000 - 5,000 = 3,000 units, representing the buffer before the business starts to make a loss.

questions.question: A company sells 8,000 units at a contribution of ₦20 per unit, and fixed costs are ₦100,000. The profit for the period is:
questions.explanation: Total contribution = 8,000 x ₦20 = ₦160,000. Profit = Total contribution - Fixed costs = 160,000 - 100,000 = ₦60,000.

questions.question: The main difference between marginal costing and absorption costing is that:
options: Marginal costing charges only variable production costs to cost units, treating fixed overhead as a period cost, while absorption costing charges both variable and fixed production overhead to cost units
Absorption costing ignores fixed costs completely
Marginal costing is used only for service businesses
There is no real difference between the two methods
questions.correct_answer: Marginal costing charges only variable production costs to cost units, treating fixed overhead as a period cost, while absorption costing charges both variable and fixed production overhead to cost units
questions.explanation: Under marginal costing, fixed production overhead is written off in full against the period's profit, whereas absorption costing includes a share of fixed overhead in the cost of each unit produced.

questions.question: When production for a period exceeds sales (closing inventory increases), reported profit under absorption costing compared to marginal costing will generally be:
options: Higher, because some fixed overhead is carried forward in closing inventory rather than charged against the period
Lower, because fixed overhead is charged twice
The same, because both methods treat fixed overhead identically
Impossible to determine without further information
questions.correct_answer: Higher, because some fixed overhead is carried forward in closing inventory rather than charged against the period
questions.explanation: Under absorption costing, fixed overhead absorbed into unsold closing inventory is deferred to a future period, reducing the current period's expense and so increasing reported profit relative to marginal costing when inventory rises.

questions.question: A cost centre, in cost accounting, is best defined as:
options: A location, department, function, or item of equipment for which costs are accumulated and control is exercised
A unit of product for which cost is calculated
The amount by which sales exceed variable cost
A fixed sum budgeted for capital expenditure
questions.correct_answer: A location, department, function, or item of equipment for which costs are accumulated and control is exercised
questions.explanation: A cost centre is an organisational segment, such as a department or machine, used to collect and control costs before they are further apportioned or absorbed into cost units.

questions.question: A cost unit is best described as:
options: A unit of product or service in relation to which costs are ascertained, e.g. a table, a tonne of cement, or a passenger-kilometre
A department in which overheads are collected
A budgeted level of fixed cost
An accounting period used for reporting
questions.correct_answer: A unit of product or service in relation to which costs are ascertained, e.g. a table, a tonne of cement, or a passenger-kilometre
questions.explanation: A cost unit is the quantitative unit of a product or service to which costs can be related, providing the basis for expressing unit costs.

questions.question: Which of the following best distinguishes cost accounting from financial accounting?
options: Cost accounting is primarily concerned with providing detailed cost information for internal planning, control and decision-making, while financial accounting focuses on reporting overall results to external parties
Cost accounting is only used by manufacturing companies while financial accounting is used by all businesses
Financial accounting records transactions in more detail than cost accounting
Cost accounting does not require any source documents
questions.correct_answer: Cost accounting is primarily concerned with providing detailed cost information for internal planning, control and decision-making, while financial accounting focuses on reporting overall results to external parties
questions.explanation: Cost accounting supplies management with detailed, often more frequent, cost data for internal use, whereas financial accounting summarises the overall financial performance and position for shareholders, regulators, and other external users.
